steps.title: Два типа глаголов
steps.html:
She is paying for a television. — действие. Его видно, и оно длится.

She thinks of it as saving. — не действие. Это то, что у неё в голове.

Глаголы мышления, чувств, желания, обладания и восприятия описывают состояние, а не действие — поэтому обычно не ставятся в Continuous.

steps.title: Какое предложение неверно?
options: I'm reading a great book about shopping.
I'm believing that shops open too early.
I believe that shops open too early.
steps.answer: I'm believing that shops open too early.
steps.why: Believe — глагол состояния, поэтому используется простая форма.

steps.title: Самые нужные глаголы состояния
steps.html:
ГруппаГлаголыПример
Мышлениеbelieve, think, mean, realize, understandI don't understand the price.
Предпочтенияprefer, like, love, hate, wantI prefer the cheaper one.
Обладаниеown, belong, have (= own)The feeling belongs to the bargain.

steps.title: Когда один глагол — и то, и другое
steps.html:
У некоторых глаголов есть значение состояния и значение действия — форма зависит от значения.

think: I think it's too expensive (мнение — состояние) · I'm thinking about buying it (процесс — действие).

have: She has two credit cards (владеет — состояние) · She's having lunch (действие).

see: I see what you mean (понимаю — состояние) · I'm seeing the manager at four (встречаюсь — действие).

options: Почему низкая цена кажется правильным решением
steps.answer: Почему низкая цена кажется правильным решением

steps.title: Why we spend
steps.html:
Прочитайте один раз. Не останавливайтесь на каждом новом слове.

On the fourth Friday in November, the shops open before it is light. It is the start of the run-up to Christmas, and every window carries a special offer. Some items are half-price; others are two for the price of one. In some cities people queue overnight to be first through the door. In the past five years there have been more than fifty injuries in these sales, and shops now employ extra security staff to keep the crowd safe.

Nobody believes they are being foolish. That is the interesting part. A shopper who pays for a television on credit does not think of it as spending; she thinks of it as saving, because the price is lower than it was last week. Researchers who study this behaviour say the feeling belongs to the bargain itself, not to the object. We recognize a good deal in a second, and by the time we understand what we have actually bought, the money has gone.

This is where Buy Nothing Day comes in. The movement is now active in more than sixty countries, and it asks for one thing only: buy nothing at all for twenty-four hours. Its supporters do not want your money — some of them give what they save to charity — and they are not asking anyone to stop shopping for ever. They mean something narrower. They want consumers to notice that the world's resources are limited, and that a purchase we do not need is harmful twice over: once when it is made, and again when it is transported across the planet.

Manufacturers have understood the message, and their answer is the guilt-free brand — a product which claims to be better for workers and for the environment. Some shoppers are convinced. Others prefer the harder question. As one campaigner admitted at a recent event, a guilt-free product is still a product, and no company has yet proved that the greenest purchase is not the one you never make.
